# Purpose

In Lab 6, you collected data from the web. In Lab 5, you developed a reproducible process for cleaning and organizing data. Now use the cleaned talk-level dataset to explore patterns and communicate one finding clearly.

The goal is not to make the largest number of plots. Use visualizations to investigate a focused descriptive question, assess the quality of the evidence, and produce one figure another person can understand.

By the end of this lab, you should be able to:
- verify that an analysis-ready dataset has the structure and quality needed for visualization;
- formulate a focused, answerable exploratory question;
- choose chart types and visual encodings that fit the variables;
- compare distributions and patterns across meaningful groups;
- improve a figure through labels, units, scales, ordering, and accessibility;
- describe what a visualization shows while acknowledging limitations.

This lab is exploratory. Do not make causal claims or treat visual comparisons as formal statistical inference.

# Setup

Use the cleaned dataset produced by the previous lab. Do not scrape the website again, and do not edit Lab 6 raw files.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

DATA_PATH = Path("data/processed/talks_clean.csv")
FIGURE_DIR = Path("figures")
FIGURE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
talks = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH)
talks.head()
```

If your cleaned file has a different name or location, update `DATA_PATH`. Do not silently substitute a different dataset.

# Part 1: Verify the data before plotting

A visualization can be technically correct but misleading if the data are incomplete, duplicated, or incorrectly typed. Begin with basic checks.

```{python}
print(f"Rows: {len(talks):,}")
print(f"Columns: {len(talks.columns):,}")
print(talks.dtypes)
```

```{python}
missing_summary = (
    talks.isna().sum().rename("missing").to_frame()
    .assign(missing_percent=lambda x: 100 * x["missing"] / len(talks))
    .sort_values("missing", ascending=False)
)
missing_summary
```

```{python}
print("Duplicate rows:", talks.duplicated().sum())
```

# Part 3: Explore the data visually

Create at least three useful exploratory visualizations. They should help investigate your question; do not create three nearly identical charts.

## Visualization 1: Examine a distribution

```{python}
if "word_count" in talks.columns:
    sns.histplot(data=talks, x="word_count", bins=25)
    plt.xlabel("Words per talk")
    plt.ylabel("Number of talks")
    plt.title("Distribution of talk length")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print("Choose an available numeric variable and update this plot.")
```

What does the distribution suggest? Are there unusually small or large observations? Does it appear symmetric or skewed?

## Visualization 2: Compare groups

```{python}
if {"session", "word_count"}.issubset(talks.columns):
    order = talks["session"].value_counts().index
    sns.boxplot(data=talks, x="session", y="word_count", order=order)
    plt.xlabel("Session")
    plt.ylabel("Words per talk")
    plt.title("Talk length by session")
    plt.xticks(rotation=30, ha="right")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print("Choose an available categorical and numeric variable and update this plot.")
```

Compare medians, spread, and potential outliers. Are group sizes large enough to make the comparison useful? Check counts rather than relying on the plot alone.

```{python}
if "session" in talks.columns:
    talks["session"].value_counts(dropna=False)
```

## Visualization 3: Examine a time pattern

```{python}
if {"talk_date", "word_count"}.issubset(talks.columns):
    yearly = (
        talks.dropna(subset=["talk_date", "word_count"])
        .assign(year=lambda d: d["talk_date"].dt.year)
        .groupby("year", as_index=False)
        .agg(median_words=("word_count", "median"),
             number_of_talks=("word_count", "size"))
    )
    sns.lineplot(data=yearly, x="year", y="median_words", marker="o")
    plt.xlabel("Conference year")
    plt.ylabel("Median words per talk")
    plt.title("Median talk length by conference year")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print("Choose an available date and numeric variable and update this plot.")
```

Describe the pattern without assuming that a trend is meaningful or that one variable caused another. Could changes in group size or data coverage affect the picture?

# Part 4: Develop one polished figure

Choose the most useful visualization from your exploration and revise it into a polished figure. Your final figure should:
- communicate one main point;
- use a chart type appropriate for the variables;
- have a descriptive title;
- label axes and include units where applicable;
- use a sensible scale and category order;
- make missing values and group sizes clear when relevant;
- use color purposefully and remain understandable without relying on color alone;
- avoid unnecessary decoration, distorted scales, and misleading emphasis.

The example below creates a polished yearly median comparison. Adapt it to your own question if another visualization is more appropriate.

```{python}
if {"talk_date", "word_count"}.issubset(talks.columns):
    yearly = (
        talks.dropna(subset=["talk_date", "word_count"])
        .assign(year=lambda d: d["talk_date"].dt.year)
        .groupby("year", as_index=False)
        .agg(median_words=("word_count", "median"),
             number_of_talks=("word_count", "size"))
    )
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
    sns.lineplot(data=yearly, x="year", y="median_words",
                 marker="o", linewidth=2, ax=ax)
    ax.set(title="Median talk length across conference years",
           xlabel="Conference year", ylabel="Median words per talk")
    ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIGURE_DIR / "lab7_final_figure.png",
                dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()
else:
    print("Adapt this code to create and save your final figure.")
```

**Final figure interpretation**
